title: Commonwealth Games Day 4 Live: Raja Muthupandi wins silver medal
summary: India rose to eighth in the Glasgow 2026 medal table with four medals: Mirabai Chanu won gold in the women's 48kg weightlifting, Raja Muthupandi claimed silver in men's 65kg, Rishikanta Singh Chanambam took silver in men's 60kg, and Jhandu Kumar earned bronze in para powerlifting. The day also featured Indian performances in relay swimming, boxing, lawn bowls and gymnastics.
content:
India rose to 8th spot in the Commonwealth Games medals standings with four medals, including one gold.

Mirabai Chanu smashed the Commonwealth Games record and won the gold medal (India’s first at Glasgow 2026) in the women’s 48kg weightlifting event. Mirabai first lifted 85kg in the snatch category to claim the Games record and more or less assure herself of a gold since she was eight kgs ahead of the next lifter at the end of snatch. Then, in the clean and jerk event, she dropped the bar for the first attempt, but nailed her second lift of 105kg to secure gold.

Here are India’s four medallists:

Follow live: Commonwealth Games Medal Tally

Earlier in the day, Rishikanta Singh Chanambam claimed a silver medal in the men’s 60kg weightlifting event, which was India’s second medal at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games. He lifted a Games record of 121 kg in the snatch event, and then added 143kg in clean and jerk to heave a total weight of 264 kg. After three largely tepid days in Glasgow, the Indian contingent’s quest to start racking up medals started in earnest with the weightlifters entering the fray today. The redoubtable Mirabai Chanu will lead India’s lifters into action on Sunday.

At the start of Sunday, India had won just the one medal at the Glasgow Games, thanks to Jhandu Kumar’s bronze medal in para powerlifting. Meanwhile, Lovlina Borgohain is also assured a medal at the Glasgow Games after the luck of the draw gave her a bye into the semi-finals.

Scroll down to read all the updates from the fourth day of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Indian relay team ends sixth after being 8th out of 8 teams after 150 metres of the first leg. But it was in the second split, by the 300m mark that India had reached 6th place.

Australia pip England to take gold. The Australians had a Games Record time too to win the gold.

Australia - 7:01.47

England - 7:04.98

Wales - 7:09.59

Scotland - 7:11.11

Malaysia - 7:23.72

India - 7:29.84

Jersey - 7:36.90

Cayman Islands - 7:49.22

So the final action of the day from an Indian perspective. Indian male swimmers are in action in the 4X200M freestyle relay final.

India quartet is:

Aneesh SUNIL KUMAR GOWDA

Dhakshan SHASHIKUMAR

Aryan NEHRA

Srihari NATARAJ

Raja Muthupandi claims a silver medal for India in the men's 65KG weightlifting event. He lifted a total weight of 286kgs, 13 kilos behind the total of Malaysia's Aznil Bin Bidin Muhamad.

Here are his attempts:

Snatch

1st lift: 126 (unsuccessful lift)

2nd lift: 126

3rd lift: 129

Clean and Jerk

1st lift: 158 (unsuccessful lift)

2nd lift: 160

3rd lift: 170 (unsuccessful lift)

Raja Muthupandi could not lift 158kg with his first clean and jerk attempt. But the coaches sent him back immediately and he nailed a 160kg lift which is a Games record. He's got one more lift left.

Favour Omovigho Agboro, coming right after Raja, heaves 160kg with his final lift. And celebrates like he's won gold. But he gets three red lights, so the lift won't count. He will have to settle for bronze.

Boxer Jadumani won by 5:0 against Collen Aaron of Scotland in the Round of 32. A smooth breeze through for the boxer, who is one of India's top medal hopefuls at Glasgow 2026.

Raja Muthupandi is currently in action in the men's 65kg event. He failed his first snatch lift of 126kg, then nailed his second lift of the same weight, and failed his third lift of 129kg. So his snatch total was 126kg.

Malaysia's Aznil Bin Bidin Muhamad lifts 130kg with his first lift, despite the flag going up and the jury reviewing his lift on video. They eventually clear it. He's coming out for a 133kg lift for his second effort. And it's a good one. For his third lift, he put up 135kg, but failed to lift.

So Raja Muthupandi was in silver medal contention with a snatch lift of 126kg. In gold contention was Malaysia's Aznil Bin Bidin Muhamad who had a Games Record lift of 133kg.

The Indian duo of Rupa Rani Tirkey and Pinki Singh have lost again via tiebreaks, this time to Amy Pharaoh and Sian Honnor in Women's Pairs Sectional Play. The result means that the Indian pair is out of the event.

Tie-break territory once again for Rupa Rani Tirkey and Pinki Singh against Amy Pharaoh and Sian Honnor in Women's Pairs Sectional Play. The England pair clawed back into the contest after losing the first set 4-3, with a 10-3 victory.

Preeti Pawar is through to the next round (quarter-finals) after a win by RSC (Referee Stops Contest). Malawi's Deborah Mtenje was given two standing counts before the referee stopped the contest in the second period.

The southpaw Preeti is playing the first round very coolly, she's staying in the centre, not rushing at the body of her opponent. All jabs from the Indian. Preeti has a height advantage which she's using well. The Indian gets a unanimous verdict for the first round. One of the five judges gives a 10-8 verdict in favour of the Indian. The other four gave her a 10-9 verdict.

India's Preeti Pawar in action against Malawi's Deborah Mtenje in Women's 54kg Round of 16 right now. Preeti has been called as one of the best bets for a medal in boxing for this Indian contingent.

In Women’s Pairs Sectional Play, India’s Rupa Rani Tirkey and Pinki Singh had the first set 4-3 against England’s Amy Pharaoh and Sian Honnor. The England pair came close to overhauling the Indians' lead.

After the second end in the Women's Pairs Sectional Play, India's Rupa Rani Tirkey and Pinki Singh surged into a 3-0 lead against England's Amy Pharaoh and Sian Honnor. It's still only the first set.

Putul Sonowal lost 1.5-0.5 to Shaun James Parnis. Meanwhile Rupa Rani Tirkey & Pinki were shortly facing Amy Pharaoh and Sian Honnor of England.

Who after Mirabai? That’s a question that has grappled Indian weightlifting for long, prompting the athlete and her coach to work on the goal. The Indian Express's Mihir Vasavda had travelled to their academy in Uttar Pradesh almost exactly a year ago, where 43 children from across the country have been lifting clean — and dreaming big.

Saikhom Mirabai Chanu was born on 8 August 1994 in Nongpok Kakching, near Imphal. Mira comes from a Meitei warrior clan. Her strength was evident from a young age, carrying heavy loads that even her elder brother struggled with.

Mirabai began weightlifting in 2008, training at the Sports Academy in Manipur. Despite financial hardships, she travelled daily to Imphal by hitching rides with truck drivers to attend training. Mirabai played her first Nationals three years later and joined the National Camp in Bangalore in 2011.

Since 2012, she has been training at NIS Patiala. At the Tokyo 2020 Olympic, she made history as the first Indian to win a silver medal in weightlifting. In gratitude, she invited the truck drivers who helped her during her early years and touched their feet as a sign of respect.

Currently, Mirabai serves as an Additional Superintendent of Police (Sports) in the Manipur Police.

Here's a look at Mirabai Chanu's achievements:

● Tokyo Games (2020) - Silver Medal

● World Weightlifting Championships (2025) - Silver Medal

● World Weightlifting Championships (2022) - Silver Medal

● Commonwealth Games (2018, 2022) - Gold Medal

● Commonwealth Weightlifting Championship (2025) - Silver Medal

● Paris Olympics Games (2024) - 4th Position

GOLD FOR MIRABAI! She dropped her first clean and jerk attempt of 105kg, but nailed her second attempt at the same weight. She had come into the clean and jerk eight kilos ahead of the second best lifter, and needed to register one good Clean and Jerk lift for the medal to be hers.

Mirabai Chanu dropped her first snatch attempt of 82kg but lifted successfully on her second and then bettered it with her third lift of 85kg to smash the Commonwealth Games record. She was eight kilograms ahead of the next lifter, Irene Jane Henry, after the end of the snatch category.

Meanwhile, in lawn bowls, Putul Sonowal was competing against Shaun James Parnis of Malta.

We're still waiting for Mirabai Chanu earlier in the session. There were a bunch of lifters who had finished all three of their attempts while Mira was yet to lift for the first time. There was a shot of her backstage, where she was sitting there grooving to music, waiting patiently.

So apparently, Mirabai Chanu had set the bar at 82 kg in the snatch category. This meant she would be last lifter in the 10-woman field to compete.

Onto the main event of the day from an Indian perspective: Mirabai Chanu in the women's 48kg weightlifting. She was going for her third gold and fourth medal overall at the CWG.

Tapan had dropped down to 13th after four rotations in gymnastics. He had scored 11.600 in single bar and earlier got 2.000 points in still rings, 12.700 in vault and 12.450 in parallel bars for a total of 48.750 at one point.

India's 4x200m freestyle relay team of Srihari Nataraj, Aryan Nehra, Aneesh Gowda, Dhakshan Shashikumar finished third in Heat 2 and moved through to the final, scheduled later that night.

Rishikanta Singh Chanambam won India a silver medal at Glasgow after he could not lift his all-or-nothing lift of 151kg but ended with a silver medal with a total weight of 264kg.

A quick look at how Rishikanta Singh Chanambam won silver:

Snatch

1st lift: 116kg

2nd lift: 119kg

3rd lift: 121kg (Commonwealth Games record)

Clean and Jerk

1st lift: 143kg

2nd lift: 148kg (unsuccessful)

3rd lift: 151kg (unsuccessful)

Mohamad Aniq Bin Kasdan of Malaysia also featured in the contest, lifting 121 kg in snatch and producing strong clean and jerk attempts. One final lift for both lifters could decide gold or silver.

Three quick lifts from Rishikanta Singh Chanambam saw him lift 118kg, then 119kg, and then 121kg, which became a Commonwealth Games record in the snatch for the 60kg weight class.

India (Rupa Rani Tirkey, Pinki Singh) lost in the tiebreak to the Namibian pairing (Amanda Steenkamp and Diana Viljoen) in the Women's Pairs Sectional Play. Despite earlier leads, heartbreak came in the tiebreaker.

India still led Group B, but England could overhaul them with a win.

As always, lawn bowls started the day's coverage. The Indian pair of Rupa Rani Tirkey and Pinki Singh faced the Namibian pairing of Amanda Steenkamp and Diana Viljoen in Women's Pairs Sectional Play.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the fourth day of the Commonwealth Games from Glasgow.

“What’s in a name?” they say. Ask Jhandu Kumar, who won India’s first medal at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. The para powerlifter, who contracted polio when he was four years old, lifted 190kg to win a bronze medal on Friday – a feat he hopes will define him, rather than his name.

Hailing from Harnaut village in Bihar’s Nalanda district, Jhandu’s name loosely translates to ‘incompetent person’ in Hindi. However, the 29-year-old, who has sold vegetables and driven e-rickshaws to fund his training, has defied every possible meaning attached to it. “Naam me kya rakha hai (What’s in a name)? I embraced this name the moment I realised that identity comes from what you do, not what you are called,” Jhandu told The Indian Express from Glasgow after winning his medal. “People used to laugh at my name. Today, it was announced from the podium with the Indian flag around me. I can’t think of a better moment in my life.”

Rishikanta Singh Chanambam won India a silver medal at Glasgow after he could not lift his all-or-nothing lift of 151kg but ended with a silver medal with a total weight of 264kg.

- 3rd lift: 121kg (Commonwealth Games record)

Raja Muthupandi claims a silver medal for India in the men's 65KG weightlifting event. He lifted a total weight of 286kgs, 13 kilos behind the total of Malaysia's Aznil Bin Bidin Muhamad.

Here are his attempts:

Snatch
- 1st lift: 126 (unsuccessful lift)
- 2nd lift: 126
- 3rd lift: 129

Clean and Jerk
- 1st lift: 158 (unsuccessful lift)
- 2nd lift: 160
- 3rd lift: 170 (unsuccessful lift)

Raja Muthupandi could not lift 158kg with his first clean and jerk attempt. But the coaches sent him back immediately and he nailed a 160kg lift which is a Games record. He's got one more lift left.

Raja Muthupandi is currently in action in the men's 65kg event. He failed his first snatch lift of 126kg, then nailed his second lift of the same weight, and failed his third lift of 129kg. So his snatch total was 126kg.

## Athlete Profile — Mirabai Chanu

Saikhom Mirabai Chanu was born on 8 August 1994 in Nongpok Kakching, near Imphal. Mira comes from a Meitei warrior clan. Her strength was evident from a young age, carrying heavy loads that even her elder brother struggled with.

Mirabai began weightlifting in 2008, training at the Sports Academy in Manipur. Despite financial hardships, she travelled daily to Imphal by hitching rides with truck drivers to attend training. Mirabai played her first Nationals three years later and joined the National Camp in Bangalore in 2011.

Since 2012, she has been training at NIS Patiala. At the Tokyo 2020 Olympic, she made history as the first Indian to win a silver medal in weightlifting. In gratitude, she invited the truck drivers who helped her during her early years and touched their feet as a sign of respect.

Currently, Mirabai serves as an Additional Superintendent of Police (Sports) in the Manipur Police.

Here's a look at Mirabai Chanu's achievements:
- Tokyo Games (2020) - Silver Medal
- World Weightlifting Championships (2025) - Silver Medal
- World Weightlifting Championships (2022) - Silver Medal
- Commonwealth Games (2018, 2022) - Gold Medal
- Commonwealth Weightlifting Championship (2025) - Silver Medal
- Paris Olympics Games (2024) - 4th Position

Who after Mirabai? That’s a question that has grappled Indian weightlifting for long, prompting the athlete and her coach to work on the goal. The Indian Express's Mihir Vasavda had travelled to their academy in Uttar Pradesh almost exactly a year ago, where 43 children from across the country have been lifting clean — and dreaming big.

## Live Coverage — Day Four

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the fourth day of the Commonwealth Games from Glasgow.

“What’s in a name?” they say. Ask Jhandu Kumar, who won India’s first medal at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. The para powerlifter, who contracted polio when he was four years old, lifted 190kg to win a bronze medal on Friday – a feat he hopes will define him, rather than his name.

Hailing from Harnaut village in Bihar’s Nalanda district, Jhandu’s name loosely translates to ‘incompetent person’ in Hindi. However, the 29-year-old, who has sold vegetables and driven e-rickshaws to fund his training, has defied every possible meaning attached to it.

> “Naam me kya rakha hai (What’s in a name)? I embraced this name the moment I realised that identity comes from what you do, not what you are called,” Jhandu told The Indian Express from Glasgow after winning his medal. “People used to laugh at my name. Today, it was announced from the podium with the Indian flag around me. I can’t think of a better moment in my life.”
